model.source: Self-reported by the reviewing session; the launcher selected Opus. Not independently confirmed by the runner.

reviewStatusBasis: All 120 rows (60 es-en, 60 en-es) are present with 10/30/20 numbering. Every row was read in full (metadata, words, notes, grammar, aligned reading, verbs) and every row received at least one recorded correction. Model review only: no human review.
sourceSemantics: LessonWord.es is always target-language text and .en is always native-language text in both files; grammar examples use es = target and en = native. In en-es, all learner-facing explanations (objective, focus, speaking task, grammar focus, word notes, verb notes, partner role) are now in Spanish; titles stay as English navigational titles and opening lines are in English (target).
summaryOfCorrections: en-es learner-facing metadata: all 60 objectives, speaking tasks and grammar-focus lines (and mixed English/Spanish focus lines) rewritten in Spanish; English-language word notes translated; one English-target opening line that was written in Spanish replaced.

English-target grammar: notes rewritten to teach English-specific points for Spanish speakers (mandative subjunctive after it is important that, present after when vs Spanish subjunctive, before + clause in indicative, want/need + object + to, single negation, recommend + -ing, explain something to someone, demand false friend, made vs did, zero vs first conditional, stop + -ing, rise vs lower, biweekly vs semimonthly). Wrong spelling rules fixed (promise, amortize).

Spanish-target grammar: wrong or misleading notes fixed (abrir called irregular, descontar called regular, personal a misidentified, de el contraction, reflexive me ayuda, enviar accent pattern, exigir register, cotizar usage, aplicar regional usage) and register made consistent (tú/usted) within scenes.

Financial terminology: pending hold vs settled/posted charge (F3, C9, M3), returned payment vs overdraft (C10), card statement vs merchant invoice and due date vs card expiry (F6), deposit receipt vs deposit slip (F4), outstanding balance vs pending transaction (C30), return of funds vs merchant refund for misdirected transfers (C7), lost-card cancellation vs unblock (C11), funds availability tied to bank policy (C4), index fund vs asset class and management fee vs total annual expense (C27).

Arithmetic corrected to match stated rates: debt consolidation $6,000 at 18% over 48 months = $176.25/month, $8,460 total, $2,460 interest (Haiku had $185); car loan $15,000 at 11.5% over 48 months = $391.34, $18,784.32 (Haiku had $391.00); added computed alternatives (36/60-month consolidation, 36-month credit union $485.42/$17,475.12). ATM shortage 300 - 200 = one missing $100 bill (Haiku said two). Budget, overdraft, fee, split and reserve figures made derivable in the reading.

Jurisdiction: retirement (C28) moved from an unnamed example country to a US 401(k) at a fictional employer with no live limits; tax/benefits (M17) moved to an IRS notice plus a fictional Texas county program with VITA specialist help; deposit protection (C25) named as FDIC-insured US deposits up to the legal limit; power of attorney (M18) placed under bank and state rules.

Scenes: contradictory or non-sequitur dialogue rebuilt (availability, lost-card timeline, delayed transfer, duplicate debit, misuse, scam, income stop, subscription dispute, household split, capstones). Every Master lesson now has an explicit complication and a practical closure. Prescriptive investment recommendations and generic warning notes removed; educators decline to pick products.

severityScale.P1: Incorrect financial concept, wrong arithmetic, missing or wrong-language translation, or a jurisdiction requirement violated.
severityScale.P2: Misleading grammar note, incoherent or unresolved scene, register inconsistency, or a learner-facing field in the wrong language.
severityScale.P3: Unidiomatic wording, imprecise gloss or minor clarity issue.

findings.correction: Rewrote the reading: A pays out $4,850 and repays 24 × 250 = $6,000; B pays out $5,000 and repays 36 × 190 = $6,840. It closes with a pero contrast. Fixed both grammar examples and the descontar and leer notes.

findings.explanation: The arithmetic was wrong: 300 - 200 = 100, but the reading said two $100 bills were missing. The operator offered to review the log before Marcos asked for it, a returned bill was also described as stuck, and the closure was vague.

The complication is now a preliminary $100 machine overage that awaits the official Monday cash balancing, and the closure names the case number and the follow-up. findings.explanation: Gabriela called her sister's account my destination account and asked the agent for a reference that was printed on her own receipt. Fixed the focus and the enviar, esperar and confirmar notes.

findings.explanation: The reading called one charge a settlement and the other an authorization, then said both were settled. That blurred the distinction between a posted duplicate and a temporary hold, which is the lesson outcome.
findings.correction: Rewrote the reading: the adviser explains what a pending authorization looks like, then shows that both charges settled on November 3 with different authorization numbers. The complication is a merchant correction notice with no reversal yet, followed by a duplicate-charge claim process and a subjunctive closure.

findings.explanation: The specialist on an official call told the customer to confirm details through the official contact; the password-change timeline was unclear; Master had no real complication.
findings.correction: Sentence 7 now checks that she called the official number; clarified the timeline; added the complication that the block stops tomorrow's rent autopay and her decision to pay at the branch.

findings.explanation: Elisa was already talking to the fraud adviser yet said she would call the number on her card. The adviser offered verification through the official number while already on it, and the borrar note contradicted the deletion in the reading.
findings.correction: Reorganized the reading: Elisa calls the card number first. The complications are a convincing message with her real name and last four digits and a second ten-minute deadline message arriving mid-call. She screenshots and then deletes the messages. Rewrote the opening line and three verb notes.

findings.explanation: The phrase un rendimiento garantizado no se puede prometer is false as a universal claim, since contractual guaranteed rates exist. The English mistranslated why does nobody else do it, the exigir note called a strong verb polite, the preguntar note was garbled, and the ending relied on an odd appeal to Bruno's risk profile.
findings.correction: Replaced the phrase with nadie puede garantizar ese rendimiento. Bruno now points out that past results guarantee nothing, refuses because he needs the money in six months, and asks about registration with a regulator. Fixed the translations and notes.

findings.explanation: The bank officer explained why the employer had stopped pay, which a bank cannot know. The couple promised not to touch the reserve while their income dropped to zero, and the missing income and runway were never quantified.
findings.correction: Rewrote the reading. The bank only sees that no deposit arrived, and HR explains that the contract ended. The figures are $2,400 of lost income, $1,500 of remaining income against $2,700 of essentials (a $1,200 gap), and a $3,600 reserve that covers 3 months, followed by a shared nosotros plan.

findings.explanation: The grammar note called me ayuda reflexive. The reading never answered the deferral request, and the late-charge reduction was not quantified.
findings.correction: Fixed the grammar note. Added the complication that the account is already delinquent, so no deferral is possible and service stops in 5 days. The figures are now concrete: 74 - 40 = 34 split as 2 × 17, a $10 late charge waived, and a temporary $35/$45 plan, with a dated commitment letter.

findings.explanation: The arithmetic did not match the stated rate: $6,000 at 18% a year over 48 months amortizes to $176.25 a month, not $185. The answer to the longer-term question was not quantified, and Master had no real complication.
findings.correction: Corrected the reading to $176.25 × 48 = $8,460 with $2,460 of interest. It now gives 60-month figures ($152.36 a month, $3,141.60 of interest) and 36-month figures ($216.91 a month, $1,808.76 of interest), and adds the complication of a $120 opening fee deducted at disbursement ($5,880 received). The final payment is explained as a rounding difference.

findings.explanation: The cancellation timeline was contradictory and never settled; the free-trial sentence was unrelated; the cancelar example (cancel before renewing, same subject) was semantically odd.

findings.correction: Corrected the payments to $391.34 × 48 = $18,784.32, and computed the credit union at $485.42 × 36 = $17,475.12. The complication is now a rate described as fixed that the paper shows turns variable after month 12. Fixed sentence 1, the grammar example and two notes.

The Spanish term reverso del cargo (charge reversal) and reversión are both used; some banks say contracargo for card disputes. Abono provisional is used for provisional credit. Confirm preferred terms.

tarifario (fee schedule) is common in Latin America; Spain may use libro de tarifas or folleto de tarifas.
